One should cause the five-fold binding (*pañcabandha*) and the eight-fold binding (*aṣṭabandha*) to be made of cotton, silk-cotton, buffalo ghee, sugar, lac, [resin], beeswax, and *sādiliṅga*. One should bind together the dregs of oil (*ucchiṣṭa*) joined with these; it is suitable for the pedestal (*pīṭha*). The eight-fold binding, when cooked and combined, is effective.

One should [perform] the unripened divine [rite] in due order. In the case of a deficiency, there is an eightfold bond for the king and the kingdom... (l. 3) ...the cold bond for all. In the north-west (Vāruṇī), [there is] the mortar... devoid of rain. In the north (Vāyavyā), there is the destruction of crops... (l. 4) ...it is said. But for one who is devoid of bondage due to negligence, [the offering of] worship, food-offerings, and so forth—[is ineffective]. First, one should always worship the Śiva-fire within the Brahma-pitcher. All ritual services [performed otherwise] are indeed fruitless... [The eight substances, the deity, the five powders, and the five forms, as well as the three powders and the three forms—these substances should be consecrated with the root-mantra along with its entirety]. The mortar has Brahmā as its presiding deity, and the pestle has Rudra as its presiding deity;
having worshipped them especially, the best of preceptors should perform the rite.

The practitioner should avoid the substances of those cooked by others, as well as their vessels; likewise, one should avoid human excrement, urine, and foot-dust. All fragrant substances should be adorned with new cloths.
Having caused the Brahmins to pronounce "an auspicious day," one should have them recite blessings;
then, one should tie on a protective thread associated with the primary *liṅga*.
One should especially wear it with a particular golden thread,
having performed a special worship as well as the consecration ceremony.
First, the installation of all [deities] is said to be the divine (*devika*) liṅga;
afterwards, the consecration at night is said to be the human (*mānuṣa*) liṅga.
One should perform the vow (*vrata*) for the temple and likewise for the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) in the center.
It should be encircled with garlands of *darbha* grass and adorned above according to the prescribed ritual.
One should have an altar prepared there with eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice;
half of that is said to be the altar, and half of that again with sesame seeds.
The Śiva-vessel (*śivakumbha*), adorned with parched grain, flowers, *darbha* grass, and new cloths, should be placed upon the *vardhanī* along with the eight Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*).
Having worshipped it with scented water, one should place five jewels and gold within it.
Having especially worshipped [the vessel] together with its beard and its lid.
One should bind all the jewels and install the primary image (*mūlabera*).
[The number of images] shall be one hundred and eight, fifteen, or twenty-five.
One should cause the ceremonial bathing (*snapana*) to be performed there and arrange [the mandala] in five colors;
one should fashion it as ninefold, fivefold, or even as a single fire-altar (*ekāgni*).
The wise practitioner should worship with perfumes and other offerings, and especially perform the fire-oblation (*homa*).
One should offer here five oblations consisting of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, and sesame seeds.
Having offered honey, all substances are especially offered;
with the *sadyojāta* mantra for the fuel-sticks (*samidh*), and with the *vāmadeva* mantra for the clarified butter (*ājya*).
Having offered the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the Aghora mantra, one should offer bamboo with the Tatpuruṣa mantra;
the wood-apple (*bilva*) with the Īśāna mantra, barley with the Heart mantra,
and especially honey with the Śivagāyatrī mantra.
Having first made the fire the mouth, one should thereafter perform the oblation.
Then, the kindling of the fire with the *jayādi* oblations and the sacrifices with the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* hymns are performed in sequence;
finally, an offering accompanied by a handful of water is made with the *śiva-mantra*.
One should feed the Brahmins there, and likewise feed those who are devoted;
one should honor the teacher there with garments, gold, and rings.
Having attained an equal status in this world, one is glorified in the realm of Śiva. Whether arising from sacrifice, service, or ritual action, the devotee who performs it shall achieve longevity,
prosperity, sons, power, and the increase of wealth and grain.
The king and the kingdom shall prosper, and all poverty shall be destroyed.

Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana-vidhi*) in the *Pratiṣṭhātantra* of the *Bhīmasaṃhitā*. Hariḥ Om. May there be auspiciousness. Salutations to the Gurus... (namas).

8a) The Conclusion of the Kṛttikā Vow (Kṛttikāvrataudyāpanam):
Now, I shall proclaim that supreme conclusion of the Kṛttikā vow.
And also the specific fruit of the worship of Kārttikeya.
And the procedure for the concluding rite (*udyāpana*), according to the rules prescribed in the *Āgamas*,
which is declared to be the most excellent, performed under the asterism of Kṛttikā.
But when devotion arises again, endowed with faith, then,
having reflected upon these words, one should perform the concluding rite (*udyāpana*) of the vow.
Without the concluding rite, one does not indeed enjoy the fruit of the vow.

Having respectfully accepted wealth from his devotees for the sake of the Subrahmaṇya rite, he should diligently complete the vow; indeed, he should conclude it with [the offering to] Kṛṣṇa alone. He who performs ablutions at sacred bathing places [should honor] the preceptor and the image-keepers.
Having performed worship of oneself, especially while observing a fast,
one should fashion an individual image for each [deity] and especially for each water-pot.
In this manner, [one should fashion] a golden image of the deity two finger-breadths in width;
when evening has arrived, having indeed bathed with pure water.
Having wrapped [the image] in a clean cloth and adorned it with white garlands,
[one should place it] together with the application of sacred ash, the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*),
and a rosary, in a garden, at the foot of a *bilva* tree, in a delightful place, or in a temple of Śiva.
Having constructed a square pavilion before that site,
measuring ten or twelve cubits and resembling the surface of a mirror;
Equipped with sixteen pillars and joined by four [gates] and twelve [arches],
it is adorned with various offerings, as well as with archways (*toraṇa*),
banners, lamps, flowers, fruits, betel nuts, sprouts, and the eight auspicious symbols.
Having fashioned nine squares in the center, or even just one square,
with a height of one cubit or even one span;
[the sections] in the cardinal directions are indeed square, while those in the intermediate directions are circular.

In the cardinal directions there is a lotus-shaped pit (*padmakuṇḍa*), or in the intermediate directions a circular pit (*vṛttakuṇḍaka*). Between Indra and Īśāna, the primary pit is hexagonal (*ṣaḍaśra*).
Having performed the smearing with cow dung, as well as the drying and baking, according to the prescribed rule— whether using nine fires, five fires, or a single fire—
one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and likewise perform the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*).
Having fed the Brahmins, he should perform the *puṇyāha* rite once again;
then, having performed breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), he should choose a twice-born man as his preceptor (*ācārya*).
One who is learned in the Vedas, of virtuous character, a householder, free from disease,
poor, tranquil-minded, accompanied by his wife, and firm in his vows.
One should choose such a Brahmin as a priest for the ritual vow— one who is perfected in the study of the Vedas and devoted to the worship of Śiva.
And the most excellent preceptor should choose one for the purpose of serving as the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*).
Under the auspicious constellation of Kṛttikā, one should remain without food during the day.
Having prepared a sacrificial altar (*vedikā*), one should arrange eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice,
half as much of rice grains (*taṇḍula*), and half as much of sesame seeds (*tila*).
In the center of that, having drawn a lotus (*padma*), [he should place] vessels surrounded by *darbha* grass, flowers, and sacrificial strewn grass—
provided with threads, covered with lids, wrapped in cloth, and containing gold.
Accompanied by mango sprouts and provided with coconuts,
there is a golden image-form measuring one niṣka.
Beginning with the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*), one should worship the *skandakumbha*,
which is joined with two powers and accompanied by the eight Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*).
One should procure all the materials for worship according to the previously stated procedure.
Having seated the teacher on a white seat in the southern quarter and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, [the practitioner],
after the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi),
himself takes his place comfortably seated by the side of his own altar.
The preceptor should perform the worship of Skanda at the place of propitiation;
he should worship with perfumes and flowers while proceeding in a clockwise direction.
Water from the Bilva tree, fragrant water, jewel-water (*ratnatoya*), golden water, snowy water,
and pure water, accompanied by various garments.
White arka, droṇa-flower, dhurdhūra, and girimallikā;
jātī, campaka, punnāga, and especially bilva leaves; karavīra, lotus, mātuluṅga, and likewise tulasī.
Sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and camphor in sequence;
gold, pearls, coral, gems, and ornaments; pure rice, milk-rice, mung-bean rice, and mustard-seed rice.
Sesame-rice, rice with lentils, and cakes, in due order,
combined with all kinds of condiments, constitute the great oblation (*mahāhavi*) consisting of all ritual substances.
One should perform worship during the first watch of the night according to the procedure for daily worship;
there, the food offering (*naivedya*) should be presented preceded by the ritual services (*upacāra*).
The preceptor, the officiating priests, and other eminent Brahmins [should do so].
The Saṃhitā-mantra, the Pada-mantra, and the Varṇa-mantra, as well as the recitation of the Kalās;
the Tattvas and the Bhuvanās, dedicated to the four Vedas;
the five-syllabled mantra, the five mantras, and the excellent fifteen-syllabled mantra.
Having worshipped the preeminent six-syllable mantra and the two goddesses of the peacock during the second watch of the night with *bilva* fruits and the thousand names, one should proceed.
The learned one [should perform worship] with the one hundred and eight names during the third watch,
and with the five Brahmans and six limbs during the fourth watch.
One should fashion a lamp-vessel together with its stand from red lac and flour;
one should place it on both sides according to one's ability, accompanied by royal insignia.
One should then devoutly offer lamps along with the two enclosures, using one's own hands.

One should likewise perform circumambulations and other rites thirty-six times; one should offer salutations that many times and perform recitation and hymns of praise that many times as well. At the end of worship during each watch of the night, one should perform the rite of fire-offering (*homa*).
One should perform all the rites beginning with the installation of the fire (*agnyādhāna*) as prescribed for the fire-sacrifice (*agnikārya*).
Alternatively, one should offer oblations by the sequence of one thousand or half of that number at each watch of the day.
In this manner, one should perform the fire offering (*homa*) primarily during the four watches of the night;
and with the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should offer it into the fire using all the ritual substances while holding the head [in reverence].
One should perform the Jaya and other rites, the installation of the fire (*abhyādhāna*), and the Rāṣṭrabhṛt offerings in due order.
Having thus performed the consecration (*jāgaraṇa*) with dances, songs, musical instruments, and various ancient hymns, when the morning becomes clear, [one should proceed].
Having bathed and become pure, one should worship Guha as before.
With a restrained mind, having accompanied the preceptor along with Brāhmaṇas,
and having washed his feet and hands, he should face northward upon the altar.
Having established these pure [images] and performed prostrations,
one should provide garments for each respective image along with grains, rice, and *śāli* paddy.
Having especially honored them with sacrificial fees and betel leaves,
one should subsequently bestow gifts upon each and every one of them.
The patron should have himself consecrated by preceptors, Brahmins, and learned scholars.
[He should wear] pure garments, the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*), and the supreme wearing of Rudrākṣa beads.
He should especially perform the tenfold gift (*daśadāna*) and feed the Brahmins in due order.
Having performed the propitiation of the deities... up to the worship of Maheśvara, one should utter the names and so forth according to their respective lineages;
having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should meditate upon Subrahmaṇya.
One should cause all the implements of the sacrifice to be given to the preceptor;
this bestows longevity, health, victory, and the abundance of wealth and grain.
Thus, whatever mortal performs this shall attain a meritorious state.
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for the conclusion of the Kṛttikā constellation rite in the Kriyāpāda of the Kumāra-tantra.

"May we know that Viśākha; may we meditate upon him who holds a spear in his hand; may Skanda inspire us. Thus, for the sake of averting misfortune and for the attainment of desired fruits, this *arghya* is offered to Guha... [the first [offering] should be]. To Jñānamūrti, Gurusvāmin, Deva, Senānī, and Nāyaka—this *arghya* is to be presented; it is proclaimed as the second. [It removes] disease, fear, poverty, and sin...

May this water-offering be for Guha, [to ward off] untimely death, fear, anger, and mental affliction. || 3 || O Lord of the Divine Army, likewise accept this water-offering which bestows long life, health, and victory, and increases sons and grandsons. || 4 || (The remainder is blank; page 16b, 13a, *kṛttikāvrataudyāpanam*, line 1) (Procedure for the Skanda-vow—) Now we shall explain the procedure for the Skanda-vow. Dālbhya said:
"O Lord of Givers, tell me of that golden vow which brings about all prosperity for men and is auspicious, performed by one desiring to please Śaṅkara.
Īśvara said:
Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! You have asked such an unsurpassed question.
I shall proclaim the majesty of the vow, the like of which has never existed before nor will ever exist again.
By what rite and by what procedure is this great Kārttikeya-vrata to be performed?
O sinless one, tell me now how its conclusion (udyāpana) should be performed according to the rules.
Īśvara:
One should perform the rite during the conjunction with Kṛttikā; having begun it then, one should practice it regularly until the end of the year, observing the prescribed rules.
Having bathed and attained purity, seated and with senses subdued day and night,
one should worship the Son of Pārvatī at evening according to the prescribed rites.
In a cow-pen, or in a temple of Śiva, or especially on the bank of a river,

or in a house within a sacred precinct (*brahmadeśa*), one should perform the rite well-prepared with canopies and other ornaments. Then, having smeared the ground with cow dung, it should be made variegated with colored powders and garlands.
And likewise the Sarvatobhadra, endowed with eighty-one squares;
having scattered five leaves and adorned it with plantain pillars,
one should place [the deity] upon a heap of rice in its center, accompanied by an *āḍhaka* measure of *śakti*.
Half of that [space] should be filled with rice, and half of that with sesame seeds;
in the center of that, there should be a lotus with petals, beautifully adorned up to the pericarp.
One should place a jar made of gold or other [precious] materials upon the grain;
it should be filled with water, joined with the five barks and sprouts, and wrapped with a thread of undecaying [silk].
Having wrapped it in a pair of garments, one should further place a fine silk cloth (*dukūla*) over it.
One should have an image fashioned there with [the value of] a hundred *niṣkas* of gold, or again, with half of that or half of that again; thereafter, one should draw a hexagon there.
In the center of that, one should place a circle, and then one should deposit the deity;
starting from the northeast corner, one should deposit the [nakṣatras] beginning with Kṛttikā.
To the east of that, one should place a peacock upon a cloth;
one should worship the six-faced god preceded by meditation and invocation,
with the sixteen types of offerings according to one's means.
One should likewise recite the names of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the *Śrīrudra*, the *Triyambaka*,
the *Ghoṣaśānti*, the *Mahāśānti*, and the *Śrīsūkta*. Then, one should [apply] musk, *rocanā*, camphor, and saffron.
One should offer flowers mixed with fragrant sandalwood and worship them with water; likewise, one should perform the worship of the limbs and present incense and lamps.
The food offering consists of the five types of delicacies and various kinds of fruits;
thereafter, betel-leaf combined with lime-powder and the waving of lights (*nīrājana*) should be presented.
Furthermore, the water of honor (*arghya*) mixed with wheat should be offered using a bamboo vessel.
Thereafter, one should offer the mantra-flowers and complete the remainder of the worship.
One should keep a vigil at night by reciting the Purāṇas and other such texts;
having fasted there according to the prescribed rules, on the following day at the time of dawn—
Having bathed and performed worship once again, one should then feed the Brahmins;
thereafter, together with many kinsmen, one should eat the food oneself from a large vessel.
Thus, upon the completion of the year-long observance, one should perform the concluding rite (*udyāpana*).
This supreme concluding rite is to be performed at the beginning, the middle, and likewise at the end.
O Brahmin, hear now its procedure as it was proclaimed by Śiva to the Goddess.
Having fashioned the constellations as water-jars, and the zodiac signs as their mouths.
[The pitchers] were provided with principal pitchers, adorned with garlands of cloth,
accompanied by images of the Six-faced One, and attended by Rākṣasas.
Then, having requested twenty-seven Brahmins who were well-versed in the Vedas and Shastras, he [appointed] the preceptor according to the prescribed ritual.
Having adorned [the disciple] and made him request [initiation], he should cause him to undertake the vow.
[The vow] is joined with the four [restraints], beginning from the cessation of worship and the avoidance of meat.

One should perform singing, dancing, instrumental music, and so forth, according to the four watches [of the day]. Having first established the sacred fire according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, [one should perform the rites] in the morning... (l. 2).
The *koṭihoma*, the *lakṣahoma*, and the *ayuta* [homa], along with... (l. 3)...
after that. Then one should prepare *paramānna* mixed with honey.
Then one should perform the oblation of clarified butter with the four [verses]...
and thereafter one should cause the food offering (*naivedya*) to be presented there.
The *nīrājana*, the mantra-flower, prostration, and circumambulation;
again the *arghya*... [and so forth].
Then, having fully honored the preceptor (*ācārya*) with garments, ornaments, and other such gifts.
Having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the image and to the officiating priests (ṛtvij) in due order.
...accordingly,
one should afterwards feed the Brāhmaṇas, provided with the five kinds of food.
And having given the sacrificial fee as prescribed...
you shall obtain all desires beyond that.
Sons, long life, prosperity, wealth, health, and whatever heart's desire you may wish for.
He obtains...
(l.3) ...just as it was formerly done by me... having [acted] formerly... [it was] performed;
thus endowed with the eight sovereign powers... (l.4)
...and even the outcastes obtain great fruit.
This is true, this is true, O man: he shall attain his desires... (l. 5)

...or [we are] victorious by our might. Thus ends the *Kārttikeyavrato dyāpana* in the *Śivadharmasāra* of the *Skānda-purāṇa*. ... (p. 19b, l. 1) Homage to Aparṇā. Homage to the Lord Guru at the forefeet. Homage to Brahmacārin at the shanks. Homage to Devasenāvallabha at the knees. I worship the thighs; homage to Haraprayatnarata. [I worship] the waist; homage to Śaravaṇodbhava. [I worship] the belly; homage to Vairilokahara. [I worship] the hands.

Salutation to the commander of the entire army; [I worship] the chest, salutation to Caṇḍabhāsura. [I worship] the heart; [I worship] the throat, salutation to the protector of the world of the gods. [I worship] the face, salutation to Subrahmaṇya. [I worship] the eyes, salutation to Agnibhū. [I worship] the ears, salutation to Kārttikeya; I worship the ear... salutation to [the forehead], salutation to Pārvatīnanda. [I worship] the mouth, salutation to Śarajanman. [I worship] the head, salutation to Ratnamauli; [I worship] the crown.

Homage to the Son of Hara. I worship his entire body. Now, the eight flowers: Homage to the Son of Īśa; *arka* flower. Homage to the Son of Gaṅgā; lotus flower (*padma*). Homage to the Beloved of the Mountain; *punnāga* flower. Homage to Paśupati; *nandyāvarta* flower. Homage to the One whose Vehicle is the Peacock; *pāṭali* flower. Homage to the Fierce One (*Ugra*); *pāṭala* and *karavīra* flowers. Homage to the One of Great Strength (*Mahābala*); *campaka* flower. Homage to the Crusher of the Host of Asuras; *droṇa* flower.

Salutation to the God of gods; I am a servant to the one who holds the *śakti* in his hand. (l. 3) This incense, consisting of ten ingredients, with *guggulu*, lamps, and mixed *candana* and *agaru*, is to be smelled by all the gods; may it be accepted. Salutation to the Compassionate One (*dayālava*). Accept this incense and lamp, O Lord of Gods, which is beautiful and combined with cow’s ghee. Today, grant the two-fold knowledge, O Destroyer of Śūra and Padmā. Salutation to the Bestower of Knowledge (*jñānaprada*). [I offer] a lamp and an oblation (*naivedya*) with fruit, O God, combined with ghee and sugar.

Mudgānna, dadhyānna, kṛsarā, sarṣapānnaka, gulānna, and paramānna—these are known as the six flavors of food (*ṣaḍrasānna*). I shall offer... O Lord of the Mountain, Skanda-deva, salutations be unto you! [This is] the food offering (*naivedya*). Accept this betel leaf (*tāmbūla*) joined with *nāgavalli* leaves, along with the *ā...ka* powder and the *kukkuṭa...* [preparation], O Son of Śiva! [This is] the betel. [This is] the water: cool, pleasing to the heart, clear, and scented with camphor.

O son of Umā, salutations to you; please accept this water. Water. (l. 3) Then, one hundred and eight [times]. Then he mutters the Vedic hymns beginning with: *āpo hi ṣṭha mayobhuvaḥ*; *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*; *pavamānaḥ*; and the verse concerning the constellations (*nakṣatra-vākya*). (l. 4) The *Rudrasūkta*, the *Bhūsūkta*, the *Śrīsūkta*, the *Puruṣasūkta*, the five *śāntis*, the *nīrājana*, the *mantra-puṣpa*, and "We worship Tryambaka. "O Agni, you are Rudra. (l. 5) *Mantra-puṣpa*. O Six-faced One, salutations to you and to the welfare of all beings.
Accept this water-offering (arghya), O Son of Mūmā; be gracious and become the bestower of boons. This is the arghya.
O Kārttikeya, Mahāsena, Śarajanman, Lord of the Gods, O destroyer of all sins, I shall offer the sacrificial oblation (*havya*). ... [to be performed]. 2. 2.
Having fully worshipped Bāhuleyendra, O Viśākha whose vehicle is the peacock, I offer this arghya to you, who are devoted to the cock-bannered deity. (3)
O Subrahmaṇya, best of gods, with beautiful limbs, bestower of happiness;
O Lord, whose essence is the power of knowledge, please accept this water of honor (arghya).
(4) For the sake of pacifying excessive sins and for the attainment of supreme excellence.
I circumambulate you; be gracious, O Six-faced One! (l.4) With this prayer:
Homage to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, wielder of the thunderbolt, ocean of compassion!
O Mahāsena, worshipped by gods and gandharvas, homage be to you!
Homage!
O you who grant desired boons along with the gods, destroyer of all sins;
O you whose face destroys the evil committed throughout seven lifetimes!
Prayer—having performed [the rites] up to the end of the mouth according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *gṛhya-sūtra* for the fire-offering... (p.21b, f.20a, l.1)

In the first watch [of the night], one should offer fuel-sticks of *palāśa*; in the second watch, an offering of fruits; in the third watch, an offering of *paramānna* (milk-rice); and in the fourth watch, with clarified butter. Then, according to the formula for the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), and by means of the formulas beginning with Kṛttikā and so forth, one should complete the remainder of the oblation with one hundred and eight or one thousand and eight offerings to Sviṣṭakṛt. Having performed worship once more, [one recites] "O Brahmin, obeisance! and "With sacrifice they sacrificed the sacrifice"—this is the concluding rite (*udyāpana*).

Having bathed the sacrificer along with his family members with water from the jar, they should then become pure and worship the lamps. Having honored the preceptor (*ācārya*) with excellent gifts such as ornaments and the like, and having given the image as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) in due order, one should give cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and so forth, according to the extent of one’s wealth. Afterwards, one should feed the Brahmins together with the five kinds of edible foods. Having given the sacrificial fee as is appropriate, one should feast together with one’s kinsmen.
The Installation of the Lord of the Field—
(l.1) Hereafter I shall explain the supreme installation of the Lord of the Field,
which serves to destroy all enemies and bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
The fifth vowel from the end, that same fifth vowel from the end, and the seed-syllable which is indeed the fifth from the end—
joined with "hari hari," this is known as the root mantra.
One should arrange the limbs of Brahmā conjoined with the fourth [vowel].
From the group of six, the first should be taken, joined with the radiant one (*arcaṣman*).
Conjoined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*, it is called the seed-syllable of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
One should fashion its limbs joined with the word ending in "mannānta.
Thus the mantra has been fully explained; now the installation is being described.
In the eastern direction of the village, or in the southeast, O Śaṅkara—
At a well-spring, a lake, in a forest, or on a mountain peak;
on the bank of a river, in a cremation ground, or at the abode of Śiva, the sanctuary of Śaṅkara.
One should establish Kṣetrapāla together with his abode,
[situated] within the divisions of qualities, having a twofold support.
One should construct either a hall measuring one and a half [units] or one that is equal in size, joined with a circular pavilion;
it may be in the Nāgara or Drāviḍa style, or it may be a peaked roof or a pavilion.
It should be provided with a rampart and well-equipped with a gate-tower (gopura).
One should especially construct the door on the south or the west.
Then, one should have an image made according to the dimensions of the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*).
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual deposition of jewels (*ratnanyāsa*) with the *hṛdaya* mantra itself.
One should effect the release of the eyes with the Netra-mantra together with the Śakti;
one should display a vessel of clarified butter while reciting the mantra "ghṛtam iṣikṣa."
One should display the vessel of honey with the mantra "This is Soma.
Having seen the strength [of the recipient], one should [offer] the sacred thread to the Brahmins by means of the root mantra.
Then, by means of the mantra "gaur dhenu-bhavya," one should show the cow and the two calves.
Having performed purification, one should then place the deity upon a water-seat.
One should construct a pavilion that is square, level, and auspicious.
Alternatively, one may construct a paved floor in the center of that area measuring nine cubits by eleven cubits.
Afterwards, O twice-born one, the brahmin should have a circular pavilion for Durgā constructed, provided with four doors and measuring twelve cubits [in size].
After dismissing the artisan, one should subsequently place five or three jars— equipped with tufts of grass, containing gold, wrapped in cloth, and filled with fragrant substances—
and install them with their respective mantras, worshipping them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should place the jar of the Lord of the Field in the center and his *prakṛti* to its left.
One should install the jars of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna.
Likewise, one should place the image of the field (*kṣetrabera*) in the northeast and the two door-guardians outside.
Krodhana and Kumbhana are on the right and left flanks;
in front of them is Śvānakumbha, while Piśākhya is said to be beyond that.
One should place twenty-seven jars starting from the east and ending with the northeast;
one should worship each with its own name-mantra and the ritual offerings.
Then, having commenced the fire sacrifice (*homa*) with sacrificial fuel (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), cooked rice (*anna*),
parched grain (*lājaka*), groats (*saktu*), milk (*kṣīra*), sesame (*tila*), mung beans (*mudga*), honey (*kṣaudra*), meat (*māṃsa*), and cake (*apūpaka*)—
these eleven substances are offered along with the limbs of Brahmā.
Or one hundred and eight, or half of that, or even half of that again.
One should offer the mantra individually for each [substance], and at the end of the substances, one should offer the *vyāhṛtis*.
One should perform meditation upon the directions, conjoined with the root mantra.
In this manner the day should be spent; at dawn, perform the installation (*sthāpana*).
Then, having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should dismiss the *bāpālika*.
Having lifted [the image] with a bed... and having removed the garments and so forth;
if it is a stone [image], [one should place it] on the bathing altar, but if it is movable, [one should place it] in the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*).
Having entered, one should worship in due order according to the rule with the root mantra.
While recollecting its root mantra, one should place the Lord of the Field (Kṣetreśa) on the left;
then, having lifted the jars in sequence, one should perform a circumambulation of the temple.
One should then place them to the east of that [Lord], following the order beginning with the principal [jar].
Having taken the seed from the pitcher, one should place it in the heart of the image;
with the water from that very pitcher, one should install the Kṣetrapāla.
Having taken the seed-syllable from the *vardhanī* vessel, one should place it as a sprinkling upon the heart;
with that water, one should cause the image to be consecrated.
Having stationed the Lords of the World (Lokeśas) surrounding the exterior of the abode,
one should place Kṣetrasena at the door in the Śāṅkara [quarter].
Having stationed a man and a dog outside that [area], and having assigned a Piśāca to the sacrificial pedestal (*balipīṭhaka*) for them, one should worship them with perfumes and other offerings.
One should worship Kṣetrapāla with perfumes, flowers, and incense;
likewise with a lamp, food offerings, betel, ornaments, and a mirror.

One should give with the heart alone; in this very manner, one should likewise offer the oblation to the Lord of the Field. Having offered the oblation to the retinue and performed the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) daily, one should perform the festival constantly, or at the three times of day, or twice a day.

Alternatively, one should perform a dance at its conclusion at a single time. Having offered the *bali* oblation to the Lord of the Field (*kṣetreśa*) daily, having recited his names and origins, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before him and strew it with *darbha* grass.
One should offer the oblation with the root mantra itself: cakes, fish, meat, honey, barley meal, parched grain, and rice mixed with fragrant substances.
Indeed, the kingdom prospers through the king's divine [fortune]; of this there is no doubt.
Then, on either the first day or the seventh day, one should perform the rite of shaving and examine the strength of the eyes.
One should set up a banner-staff and have an inscription written upon it:
"Hoist [this] especially every seven days."
One should perform the installation of the Lord of Yoga and worship Him with scents, flowers, and so forth;
at the conclusion of that, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) according to the sequence beginning with sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*).
The fuel sticks are offered with the *Sadyojāta* mantra, while the clarified butter (*ājya*) is offered with the *Vāmadeva* mantra.
Having offered the *caru* oblation with the *aghora* mantra, and having offered fragrance with the *nara* mantra;
having offered curd with the fifth [mantra], and the cake (*apūpa*) with the *hṛdaya* mantra;
having offered honey with the *śiras* mantra, one should offer the *vyāhṛti*s for each [of these].
One should offer the bali oblation in the evening and in the morning, having first performed the fire-sacrifice (homa) at its conclusion with various substances:
namely, pure rice, rice mixed with sesame, rice mixed with mung beans, and molasses water.
One should offer, in sequence, food made of mung beans, milk-rice, and meat;
indeed, food consisting of seven [grains] should be given while reciting the respective mantra for each.
First is Bhūtarātra, and the second is Guṇarātra;
the fifth is Gaṇanātha, and likewise the sixth is Rākṣasa.
Then there is Kṣetrapāla with his attendants; these seven groups are the presiding deities.
At its conclusion, one should perform a festival adorned with all ornaments.
On the day of Rākṣasa, one should proclaim the commencement of the battle.
During the seven-day period, there shall be a powder-festival, and at its end, one should perform the Tīrtha ceremony.
One should perform the raising of the banner and then have the ceremonial bathing performed;
there, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings.
The mortal who acts in this manner shall attain a meritorious state.
The installation of the Lord of the Field has been declared; now hear the installation of the Sun.
Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the installation of the Lord of the Field (*kṣetreśasthāpanavidhi*) in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Pratiṣṭhātantra*, belonging to the *Bhīmasaṃhitā*.
The Installation of the Sun (*ravisthāpana*). Now I shall explain in detail the supreme installation of the Sun.
It brings about all accomplishments, is meritorious, and bestows benefit upon the entire world.
Longevity, health, victory, sons, and the attainment of wealth—
whether in a village, a city, a town, or a royal capital.
In a hamlet or a small village, on the bank of a river or a pond, in a forest or even in a house, in a temple of Śaṅkara or a sanctuary of Śaṅkara;
in the northeast, the east, or likewise the southeast of the villages.
Between Indra and Agni, one should fashion the temple of the Sun, measuring four hundred cubits [in extent],
provided with an equal-sized pavilion,
enclosed by a wall on the outside, and equipped with a gateway (gopura).
One should arrange the gateway at half of that [measurement], facing west,
in accordance with the inner sanctum and together with the characteristics of the house-gates and archways.
Whether it be made of clay, stone, wood, or likewise of precious minerals,
fashion it according to the previously mentioned procedure, with a minimum height of ten tālas.

One should perform the rite of sowing the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) prior to the day of the consecration; having prepared either a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or a leveled altar (sthaṇḍila), one should place the pedestal (piṇḍikā) upon it.
Having recited the mantra of the planets, one should place the nine gems;
having placed the Sun upon that, make it very smooth and very firm.
One should also place Uṣas, Pratyuṣas, and the [images] of Suparṇa.
On a day joined with the constellation Netra, having inspected the axle with the Netra-mantra,
the work should be performed by the artisan together with the striking of the golden needle;
one should then show a cow with her calf and her limbs smeared with honey and ghee while reciting the respective mantra.
Having recollected the seed-syllable of the Sun, one should display a heap of grain;
then, having performed purification with the five earths and the five products of the cow, [one should worship] the Sun.
One should perform the circumambulation of the village; then, having cooked [the materials] in water...
one should construct a pavilion for the white palace, provided with sixteen pillars, and a vessel equal in height to its name.
Having constructed eight squares by eight in the center, the intermediate directions are formed by four cells;
it should be eight finger-breadths in height, free from depressions or elevations.
In the center of the three excellent compartments, that quadrangle is the fourteenth;
for all [the fires], there is one kuṇḍa at each corner, shaped like a lotus.
One should perform the dismissal of the artisans with a measure of one cubit;
then, having smeared [the ground] with cow dung, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited.
Then, having performed the Vāstuhoma, carry out the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa). Afterwards, one should feed the Brahmins and dispose of the remnants.
One should smear [the ground] with cow dung and again perform the rite for a day of merit;
thereafter, one should construct a pavilion adorned with divine ornaments.
One should have a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) constructed in the center of the altar with jewels and grains;
there, one should prepare a bed according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having emerged from the water and performed purification with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should worship the Sun.
One should smear it with saffron, red sandalwood, and *kurvi*;
having joined it with a brush (*kūrca*), one should wrap it in a red cloth.
Then, having tied a protective thread (*rakṣāsūtra*), one should lay it upon a raised bed.
Having filled a jar with water from the Droṇa river and stirred it with pomegranate seeds, one should wrap it with a red thread and wash [the disciple] while reciting the Heart mantra.
One should fill it with scented water and wrap it with a red cloth;
one should place a ruby in the center and deposit a bundle of kuśa grass (*kūrca*) within it.
One should place the supreme establisher on the right side of the head;
then, having meditated upon him in the form of the Sun, one should deposit his root-mantra into that jar.
The first seed-syllable is said to be the letter *ṣa*, ending with the nasal (*anta*), conjoined with fire (*vahni*), joined with the second vowel, and endowed with the *bindu* and *nāda*.
Having extracted the letter *pū* together with its offspring (*vatsā*), it is further endowed with fire and *māyā*.
The second seed-syllable is said to be joined with the syllable *oṃ*.
The third seed-syllable is said to be the letter *ṣ* at the end [of the row] conjoined with the *visarga*.
The fourth seed-syllable is said to be the letter *ṣ* at the end [of the row] endowed with the sixth vowel.
The second [vowel] joined with the letter following *ma*,
conjoined with fire, is said to be the fifth seed-syllable.
The sixth seed-syllable, ending with the letter *bha*, is here called the six-syllabled [mantra];
it is joined at the beginning with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and joined at the end with the word of salutation (*namaḥ*).
One is purified from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin by the recitation of the mantra.
One should fashion the limbs of Brahmā joined with the sound *nāda* and so forth.
This has been declared as the root mantra; now hear the seed-syllable of Dawn (*uṣā*).
The fifth letter from the vowel class should be taken, conjoined with the Bindu and the Nāda.
One should take the first [letter] from the group of six, known as the seed-syllable of Uṣā;
it is conjoined with the seed-syllable of Fire and endowed with the Bindu and Nāda.
The seed of the dawn has been declared, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Two jars, filled with half a *droṇa* of water and joined with threads and other [materials],
should be placed in succession within the solar jar in remote locations.

One should place eight water-pots all around, in order starting from the east; one should then worship them in sequence, beginning with Soma and ending with Ketu. Then, one should commence the fire-oblation according to the procedure prescribed for the ritual of the sacred fire.
My preceptor is primarily [the officiant] for me; however, the presiding deity (mūrtipāt) is in another sacrificial pit.
The teacher is one whose soul is well-pleased, born from a family of Śiva-brahmins.
Wearing a red upper garment and pure red clothing,
and equipped with a red sacred thread, the preceptor should perform the fire oblation.
One should perform the fire oblation with fuel sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, milk, curd, sesame, and barley,
starting from the lotus and ending on the left, using the respective mantras.
And Vaikartana [and] Divākara.
These indeed are the presiding deities (*adhidevatā*) of the twelve *kuṇḍas*.
One should install twenty-seven jars in the midst of the *paiśāca* position.
Having worshipped [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should worship Nandin and the others.
White *arka* or red [flowers] are prescribed as the *argha* for all; likewise, sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*) are prescribed.
One should offer a hundred, or half of that, or half of that again, and at the conclusion of the substances, one should perform the *vyāhṛti* oblation.
One should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) one hundred times with the mantra beginning with *sūryalekhā*.
In this manner, the night should be spent; at dawn, perform the installation.
Then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* while recollecting the root mantra, one should extract the *āśaya*... and place it, [marked with] *baṃ*, immovably in that which is called the bath.
One should install Acala and Devika within the inner sanctum;
one should place the Sun in the middle of those two, conjoined with the two Śaktis.
One should then perform the placement of the six limbs of that respective Brahman upon its body.
Having removed the jars, one should place them upon red śāli rice in front of the image.
Taking up the mantras of the jars, one should assign Sūrya and Candra [to them]. Then, one should perform the consecration with that water using the heart-mantra.
Having placed the two *śakti* mantras in the sequence starting from the south,
one should sprinkle [the disciple] with the water contained in each respective jar while reciting the corresponding mantra.
One should cause the offering of perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings,
as well as betel leaves and all other items, with their respective mantras.
One should install the retinues, beginning with Soma, in their proper order.
Perform daily the offering to the retinue, the fire sacrifice, and the perpetual festival.
At the conclusion of that, one should bring about happiness through whatever specific rite has been observed;
thereafter, one should cause a festival to be held for as long as seven days.

A nine-day festival is declared the best, a seven-day one would be middling, and a five-day one is declared the lowest; thus the festival is of three kinds. One should cause it to be performed according to the prescribed rule, beginning with the raising of the banner and ending with the pilgrimage to the sacred sites (*tīrtha*).
Afterwards, one should honor the teacher with grain, clothing, gold, and other offerings.
The mortal who acts in this manner goes to the world of the Sun. Thus has been declared the installation of Āditya; now hear the installation of Nāgeśa.
Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the installation of the Sun in the Kriyāpāda of the Pratiṣṭhātantra, within the Bhīmasaṃhitā, concerning the classification of causes.
The Establishment of Nāgeśa. (p.31b, f.30a) (l.1)
Now I shall fully describe that supreme installation of Nāgeśa,
which serves to destroy all diseases and to increase the prosperity of kings and kingdoms.
The letter *dhā*, ending with the thirteenth [consonant], conjoined with the seed-syllable of fire (*ra*),
and further joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*, is known as the root mantra.
One should arrange the limbs of Brahmā joined with that very [syllable] ending in *ya*.
The fifth letter of the *a*-group should be taken, accompanied by the bindu and the nāda.
The mantra of Uragavyā consists of the letters *da*, *a*, *n*, *ta*, *n*, joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*).
This is declared to be the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Nīgeśa, which destroys all diseases.
Thus the mantras have been fully explained; now the installation (*sthāpana*) is being described.
In the southwest, northwest, or northeast of the village;
on a riverbank, in a cow-pen, or on the shore of a great river; near a tree, on a mountain, or in a forest.
In the house, or on the bank of a pond, to the southwest of the abode of Śiva, or to the northwest, or in the northeast, or in the middle of the temple.
One should then install the Lord of Serpents either to the south or to the north;
[the distance] should be seven cubits, or according to the star-measurement of the temple.
Its height should be equal to that [width], or half, or double;
it may be a pinnacle (*kūṭa*), or a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), or even a *nandyāvarta* shape.
It is joined with the walls of the enclosure and provided with a gate-tower (*gopura*).
Then, one should have an image made according to the measurement of a *garbhagṛha* (the inner sanctum),
whether it be made of metal, stone, clay, or wood;
it should have two eyes, two arms, be peaceful in appearance, and adorned with all ornaments.
Adorned with a crown and a jeweled casket, with palms joined in reverence,
[he is] endowed with a camel and stands upon a lotus seat.
Urageśī and Nāgeśī are situated to the south and north;
one should visualize them with forms adorned with youth and beauty.
One should fashion various forms of many colors separately and individually,
[endowed] with the union of the five heads.
Endowed with a body like the sky, joined with a single neck, and possessed of ten ears, [he has] the serpent... (l. 3).
Then, in the regions of the head, he is encircled by a hood.
One should properly perform the consecration ceremony during the period of the sun's northern course.
The best of preceptors should install [the image] in the presence of Rudra according to the supreme method of the *Pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.
Then one should perform the deposition of the jewels... [where it may be]. One should perform the opening of the eyes while reciting the respective mantra for each eye.
[That which is] made of flour, combined with gold, [and mixed] with honey and clarified butter... (the final folio is broken; p. 33a, l. 1)...
having performed purification by that very [means], thereafter...
Having wrapped it with a new cloth, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) with water;
then, one should transport it to the center of the dwelling. In the middle, one should construct a paved floor (*kuṭṭima*) four finger-breadths in height.
To the east of that, one should make a square marked with the characteristic signs...
[one should prepare] the sacrificial mound (*maṇḍala*) and then arrange the bed.
Having emerged from the water and performed purification for the Lord of Nagas (*nāgeśa*) with his own mantra, one should proceed.
Having performed the purification, what [should be] the auspicious rite (*kautuka*)?
Having fashioned the fivefold egg-born [image], one should place it upon the bed.
One should install the jars starting from the eastern direction.
In the center, however, there is the Nāga-jar, and on both sides are the two Śakti-jars.
Around [the central vessel], there are eight jars for the presiding deities beginning with Ananta: ...

1) (Bhadrakālī-sthāpanam:
Listen; I shall declare the installation of Mahākālī, which bestows all perfections.
During the period of the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day.
One should avoid a movable sign (*cararāśi*) even when it is endowed with auspicious [planets] and the like;
whether in a village, a city, on a mountain, or in a royal capital.
Is it better to practice on the bank of a pond, in a forest, on the bank of a river, in a cremation ground, at the foot of a *caitya* tree,
or on a great highway in a village?
Or is it in a village and the like that is auspicious, or perhaps in a place sacred to Agni or Śaṅkara?
One should install [the image] provided with a temple in the southwest, or in the northwest, or even in the abode of Īśvara; one should worship it according to the prescribed rite.
This supreme task for the deity must be performed by a Śiva-brahmin.
By that very [means], the kingdom is honored, there is an abundance of food, and diseases are destroyed.
For one who touches another caste, there shall be fear of disease and thieves;
among men, the Brāhmaṇa is the best, and among Brāhmaṇas, the twice-born Śiva.
There, [the hall] should be six *hasta* in width, with a height double that [width],
provided with a half-pavilion (*ardhamaṇḍapa*), and enclosed by walls and a rampart.
One should cause a temple of Īśvara to be constructed, provided with a gopura gateway;
it may have its entrance on the east, the west, or even the north.
One may cause it to be made of wood, stone, or even brick.
Having two arms, or four arms, or even endowed with eight hands.
The eighteenth is the Hasta [mudrā], and likewise the Pretavāhana;
first is the Ratnavinyāsa, and second is the Netramokṣaṇa.
The third is the Vision, and the fourth is the Accomplishment of the Image;
adorned with all ornaments, one should perform the circumambulation of the village.
Afterwards, one should perform the ritual immersion of the image in water (jalādhivāsana), and following that, the sacrifice and worship;
one should then construct a square pavilion in front of the assembly members.
...one should construct an altar (*vedikā*) resembling the interior of a mirror.
One should cause sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) in the shape of a vulva (*yoni*) to be made in the four directions starting from the east.
One should also prepare a bathing altar in the west or the north,
having smeared it with cow dung and adorned it with all ornaments.
The preceptor should prepare a bed in the center with five cloths;
having emerged from the water and performed purification, especially for Kālī,
he should wrap her in a red cloth and then bind the *kautuka* thread.
One should encircle with the Astra-mantra a jar filled with thirty prasthas [of grain],
fill it with pure water, a cloth, a bunch of kuśa grass, and gold.
Having meditated upon Kālī and recited her mantra, one should place eight jars around it.
One should place the nine powers, beginning with Vāmā, within the central jar;
likewise, one should place the jar of the retinue together with the network of powers.
Having worshipped [the deity] individually with perfumes and other offerings up to the food offering (*naivedya*),
one should commence the rite of fire-oblation (*homakarma*) according to the path taught in the *Vahnimārga*.
One should offer fuel-sticks of *palāśa* in the eastern portion, *khadira* in the south,
*śamī* in the western pit, and *audumbara* in the northern one.
In the primary *yonikuṇḍa*, however, one should offer *akṣa* as the fuel-sticks.
One should perform the fire-oblation with sacrificial fuel, boiled rice, parched grain, mustard seeds,
barley, sesame, bean cakes, molasses cakes, and likewise sesame cakes;
beginning with the *sadyas* [mantras] and ending with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should offer these with the mantras.
Having offered one hundred oblations for each [deity], one should offer the *vyāhṛti* at the conclusion of the substances;
the worship and the fire-oblation at the two junctions [of the day] should be accompanied by dance and song.
At the four gates, the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images, should recite the Śaiva mantra according to the sequence of the four Vedas; then he should perform the two ablutions.
Then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* with the mantra "O Agni, [this has been] well-sacrificed" (*sviṣṭam agne*),
he should lift up the goddess Kālī from her bed, fully adorned with all ornaments.
If it be made of metal, one should enter the bathing altar; if it be made of stone, one should enter the temple.
Then, having performed the placement of the jewels (*ratnanyāsa*), one should begin the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*).
This should be done either with the five Brahmans and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) or according to the sequence of the deposition of the paths (*adhvanyāsa*).
Having extracted the primary jar, which is endowed with the eight powers.
Having taken up the mantras from the jars, one should place them upon the heart of the image;
then Mahākālī herself should sprinkle it with the water from that very jar.
One should worship [the deity] adorned with all ornaments and with perfumes, flowers, and so forth. From the east to the northeast, there is the consecration with eight jars.
The mantra-practitioner should establish [the deity] with mantras and worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
[he should offer] water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya offering together with coconut fruits,
incense, lamps, food offerings, betel leaf, and sugarcane stalks.
Clad in red garments, adorned with red flowers and all ornaments—[one who is] unattached to the universe is thus described. One should mutter the fivefold *īkṣya*:
the fan, the chowrie, the parasol, the mirror, and likewise the sandals.
Having offered the *parivāra-bali* and even the boiled rice for the goats,
one should perform the daily fire-ritual (*nityāgnikārya*) at the conclusion of the worship, and thereafter the daily festival (*nityotsava*).
Thereafter, one should feed the Brahmins and perform the ten types of gifts and so forth in due order;
afterwards, one should celebrate a festival accompanied by dance and song.
Having first established the great banner, [he performed] the Paiśāca...
(l.4), as well as the sacrifice-worship, the sacrificial oblation, and the binding of the protective thread.
Having offered the *bali* at the conclusion of the *homa* every day, both morning and evening,
one should worship the *ācārya* there with garments, gold, and rings.
The mortal who acts in this manner shall attain a meritorious state.
