[The *Gaṅgāstotra* composed by Kālidāsa is complete. (p. 65b, f. 81a, *Kālīpratiṣṭhā*, l. 1) (*Kālīpratiṣṭhā*): Her left foot rests upon a lotus pedestal; her other hand holds a trident; she is adorned with necklaces and armlets.
I constantly meditate upon the form of Śivakālī, who is worthy of supreme worship by the immortals, and whose right hand is extended downward; victory to her!

On the ground, having worshipped Śiva-Sūrya as if it were permanent in the space between the directions of the wheels and the wind, and having performed the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*) and sipping water (*ācamana*), one who has performed the ritual of total identification (*sakalīkaraṇa*) should prepare the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*). Having sprinkled [it] with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), [one should offer]: in the east—*oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the Peace Archway (*śāntitoraṇa*); *oṃ*, salutation to the Ṛgveda; salutation to the Kṛta Age. On the trident: salutation to Gaṅgā; salutation to Mahālakṣmī; salutation to Narmadā; salutation to the *a*-group (*avarga*).

Salutation to the *kavarga* [consonant group]. On the southern and northern branches: salutation to Nandin; salutation to Kuṇḍalī-śakti; salutation to Mahākāla; salutation to Pīṭhanī-śakti. In the center: salutation to Śāntikalā; salutation to Umā; salutation to Dehinī-śakti. On the two branches: *saṃ* salutation to Somā; *buṃ* salutation to Budhā. Having offered these perfumes, unbroken rice, flowers, and lamps: *aṃ* salutation to Agni; salutation to Svāhā-śakti.

On the south: *namaḥ* to Bhūtitoraṇa; *namaḥ* to the door of the Vidyā-kalā; *namaḥ* to the Yajurveda; *namaḥ* to the Tretā-yuga. On the trident: *namaḥ* to Yamunā; *namaḥ* to Sarasvatī; *namaḥ* to Sindhu. On the southern and northern branches: *namaḥ* to Bhṛṅgin; *namaḥ* to the Hryādinī-śakti; *namaḥ* to Vināyaka; *namaḥ* to the Bhṛṅgiṇī-śakti. In the center: *namaḥ* to Vidyākalā; *namaḥ* to Yama.

Salutation to Kālakaṇṭhī. On the two branches: salutation to Bṛhaspati; salutation to Bhārgava; salutation to the *ca*-group [of consonants]; salutation to Gaṅgā. Having offered these [deities] perfumes, unbroken rice, incense, and lamps: salutation to Nirṛti; salutation to the Śakti Dehinī; salutation to Viṣṇu; salutation to Mahālakṣmī; salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the site (*vāstuvādhipati*). Having offered perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps.

In the west—(l.2) salutation to Balatoraṇa; salutation to the door of the Nivṛtti-kalā; salutation to the Dvāpara-yuga; salutation to the Sāmaveda. In the trident—salutation to Godāvarī; salutation to Umā; (l.3) salutation to Kāverī. On the southern and northern branches—salutation to Vṛṣabha; salutation to Bhadrādevī; salutation to Skanda; salutation to Śaśisuta; salutation to Mahālakṣmī. (l.4) [To] Śāśvaya? salutation to the group of consonants beginning with *ha* (hitavarga); salutation to the group beginning with *pa* (pavarga).

Having offered incense, flowers, incense-smoke, and lamps: *namaḥ* to Vyūha; *namaḥ* to Ghorāśakti; *namaḥ* to Gaṇeśvara; *namaḥ* to Vallabhā. Having offered incense, flowers, incense-smoke, and lamps. In the north: *namaḥ* to Ārogyatoraṇa; *namaḥ* to the door of the *Pratiṣṭhā* kalā; *namaḥ* to the Kali Yuga; *namaḥ* to the Atharvaveda. At the trident: *namaḥ* to Śroṇabhadrā; *namaḥ* to Bhāgīrathī; *namaḥ* to Tuṅgabhadrā.

On the southern and northern branches: *devyai namaḥ* | *caṇḍāyai namaḥ* | *rūpiṇyai namaḥ*. In the center: *pratiṣṭhākalāyai namaḥ* | *kuberāya namaḥ* | *gambhīraśaktaye namaḥ*. On the two branches: *rāhave namaḥ* | *ketave namaḥ*. [As for the letters: *yavargāya namaḥ* | *śavargāya namaḥ*. Having worshipped the *astravardhanī*, [one worships] in the northeast: *īśānāya namaḥ* | *maharṣiṇīśaktaye namaḥ*.

Salutation to Brahmā. Salutation to Sarasvatī. Salutation to the Guru Sadāśiva. Salutation to the Guru Ananta. Salutation to the Guru Śrīkaṇṭha. Salutation to the Guru Ambikā. Salutation to the Guru Guha. Salutation to the Guru Kṛṣṇa. Salutation to the Guru Dhātṛ. Having thus worshipped the seven Gurus and offered perfume, flowers, incense, and a lamp, one should worship the door in the west as usual.

On the banners of the directions starting from the east: *khaḍgāya huṃ phaṇnamaḥ*. In the center: *oghoraśaktaye namaḥ*. On the flags starting from the east: *kumudāya namaḥ*; *kumudākṣāya namaḥ*; *puṇḍarīkākṣāya namaḥ*; *vāmanāya namaḥ*; *śaṅkukarṇāya namaḥ*; *sannetrāya namaḥ*; *sumukhāya namaḥ*; *supratiṣṭhāya namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped, [one worships] in the directions starting from the east: *oṃ hāṃ hetukāya namaḥ*; *tripuraghnāya namaḥ*.
Salutation to Vahni. Salutation to Yamajihva. (L. 5) Salutation to Kāla. Salutation to Karālin. Salutation to Ekahṛdaya. Salutation to Bhīma.
The meditation (*dhyāna*):
[He] whose face is terrifying with fangs, and who has a serpent as his sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).
"Equipped with a bell-metal sword, they are proclaimed as the foremost of the Hetukas.

Having meditated thus, having worshipped the Kṣetrapāla, and having contemplated them as being satisfied, [one offers oblations] in the case of trembling and other such phenomena occurring in the upper part of the mandala: "Homage to the Earth-element! Homage to the form of Sadyojāta! In the case of grasses: "Homage to the Water-element! Homage to the secret Vāmadeva! In the case of bonds: "Homage to the Fire-element! Homage to the heart of Aghora! In the case of bamboo poles: "Homage to the Air-element! Homage to the face of Tatpuruṣa!"

On the pillars: having worshipped with "Obeisance to the principle of space (ākāśatattva)" and "Obeisance to the head of Īśāna," one should visualize the pavilion of power (śaktimaṇḍapa). Looking at it with that [divine] vision, and striking with the remaining door, one should install twenty-seven jars on the two side-doors. In the northern jar of the eastern door:
[one should worship] the four-faced, four-armed, black-colored Mahābala, holding a banner, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, with Śānti as his sacred thread, adorned with serpents.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the door of the Śāntikalā. In the eastern pitcher of the southern door: [one should visualize] the one who possesses a spear, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus; who resembles blazing lightning and fire; who has four faces, four arms, a black complexion, and great strength.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the door of the Vidyā-kalā. In the southern pitcher of the western door: [I worship] Nivṛtti, who has the luster of molten gold, is adorned with four faces and a crescent moon, and holds a vajra, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus; she is proclaimed as the bestower of renown.
Salutation to Nivṛttikalādvāra. In the western pitcher of the northern door:
[He who is] resembling pure crystal, with two faces and four arms, holding a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, adorned with jewels of the Pratiṣṭhā [kalā].
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the door of the *pratiṣṭhā* level. Having worshipped according to the ritual rules, [one should worship] at the northern pitcher of the eastern door: obeisance to Ambikā.
The visualization (*dhyāna*): she has one face and two arms, and is adorned with all ornaments.
[He is] endowed with a crown of matted locks, dark-complexioned, and in the full bloom of youth.

(l.2) To the south: *Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to Gaṇāmbikā. To the east of the southern gate: obeisance to Gaṅgā; to the west, obeisance to Gaurī. To the south of the western gate: obeisance to Umā; to the north, obeisance to Aiśvaryā. To the west of the northern gate: obeisance to Manonmanī; to the east, obeisance to Dhāriṇī. In the four directions starting from the east, [they are] yellow in color, with garments and ornaments, and have the swan as their vehicle. (l.4) To the east: obeisance to Dhāriṇī. In the four directions starting from the east—yellow-colored garments and ornaments, and likewise the swan as the vehicle.
Four-armed, three-eyed, and likewise four-faced;
granting fearlessness and boons, holding a rosary and a water-pot;
adorned with all ornaments and graced by a crown of matted hair.
Having meditated thus: "Homage to Brahmā!
Three-eyed and four-armed, endowed with a pure complexion, joined with a crown of matted hair, and accompanied by his one wife."
Having likewise made Maheśvarī her vehicle, she holds the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, as well as a deer, an axe, and water.
Salutation to Māheśvarī!
[He who is] one-faced and two-eyed, adorned with a crown and a casket,
bearing a vajra and a śakti, and decorated with all ornaments.
Homage to Kaumārī!
She is described as holding a conch and a discus, adorned with golden ornaments,
seated upon Garuḍa, and endowed with a lotus seat.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vaiṣṇavī!
She holds a trident, a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons; she is adorned with a basket-shaped crown and all ornaments, and is likewise mounted upon a buffalo.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vārāhī!
She holds a vajra and a spear, is mounted upon an elephant,
is endowed with a rosary, and is beautiful in all her limbs.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Māheśī!
She has three eyes and hair standing erect; likewise, she holds a hand-drum and a noose, as well as a skull and a trident in her hands, and has a corpse for her vehicle.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Cāmuṇḍī!
She has one face and four arms, is adorned with serpent ornaments,
wears red garments, and is equipped with a trident and a noose.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Durgā. Salutation to Mahālakṣmī. Salutation to Sarasvatī. Having thus worshipped [them], and having worshipped the door-keepers in the west as is customary, [one should worship]: salutation to Gaṅgā; salutation to Yoginī; salutation to Ḍākinī; salutation to Yamunā; salutation to Mahālakṣmī; salutation to Sarasvatī; salutation to Narmadā; salutation to Padaṅgā; salutation to Bhuvaṅgā; salutation to Vimalā.

......ve namaḥ | Siṃhāyai namaḥ | Astradvārapālāya namaḥ | Vāstupānidhipatibrahmaṇe namaḥ | Having thus worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having expelled the obstacles residing in the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms, ... having worshipped the Weapon [mantra] and entered, and having proceeded by way of circumambulation, one should worship the Lord of the Site (Vāstunātha) in the southwest.

Having entered from the south of the altar facing north, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), the purification of the site (*sthānaśuddhi*), the purification of the materials for the special *arghya* offering, and the purification of the mantras. Having performed the preparation of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) as before, and having performed their respective worship, [one should place offerings] on one's own forehead, throat, and the region down to the feet: "Obeisance to the Śiva-principle (*śivatattva*); obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the Śiva-principle; obeisance to the Knowledge-principle (*vidyātattva*)."

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the lord of the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*); obeisance to the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*); obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the principle of the self"; and having placed Śiva—who possesses his seat and the limbs of Brahmā—as the pervader of the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*), one should place the hand of Śiva [upon the disciple]. Having adorned oneself as one's own form, complete with garments and crown, one should contemplate, "I am Śiva. Then, taking up the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*) and consecrating the scattered offerings (*vikira*), one should proceed.

Standing in the southwest (nairṛta), having performed the consecration through inspection and other rites, having scattered the *vikirā* offerings, and having gathered up the bundle of *kuśa* grass, one should provide a seat for the *vardhanī* vessel in the northeast. Having worshipped the *vāstu* deity, one should worship Lakṣmī at the western gate as before. Then, having worshipped the auspicious jar (*śivakumbha*), the weapon (*astra*), the *vardhanī*, and the movable seat (*calāsana*), and having worshipped Śakti and the other world-protectors (*lokapāla*) in their respective directions, one should cause [the officiant] to hear the command of Śiva according to the [appropriate] knowledge.

Recalling the *astradurga* mantra, one should rotate [the vessel] with the *mela*. Having placed the eastern pitcher (*kumbha*) first and the *vardhanī* afterwards, and having performed worship upon the stable seat (*sthirāsana*) for both the pitcher and the *vardhanī*, one should address [the deity]: "O Lord of the sacrifice born from the union of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*, ... forgive me out of compassion for your devotees. Then, having established the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaṭga*), the water of honor (*arghya*), and the water of restraint (*nirodhārghya*).
Having offered the food offering (*naivedya*) and betel leaf (*tāmbūla*), one should then [offer] in the corners of the altar—from *Dharma* to the end of *Padma*—saying: "Obeisance to Parāśakti.
The visualization (*dhyāna*):
[She has] one face and four arms; her right hands hold a *kuśūla* and a beautiful noose (*pāśa*).
O Mañjuśivamahākālī, who holds a hand-drum and a skull-bowl in your hands, homage be to you!

Having thus invoked: ... *namaḥ* to Tārā—on the head; *namaḥ* to Vidyā—on the face; *namaḥ* to Mūrti—in the heart; *namaḥ* to Śuddhā—in the throat; *namaḥ* to Rajā—in the left arm; *namaḥ* to Medhā—in the right arm; *oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ* to Svadhā—in the stomach; *namaḥ* to Svadhātī—in the navel; *namaḥ* to Varmaṇā—in the vulva; *namaḥ* to Kapālī—in the right thigh; *namaḥ* to Pālinī—in the left thigh.

Salutation to Tṛṣṇā—on the right knee. Salutation to Dhṛti—on the left knee. ... [name] salutation—on the right calf. Salutation to Mati—on the left calf. Salutation to Prajā—on the right buttock. Salutation to Śāntā—on the left buttock. Salutation to Mūrti—on the left side. Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to Kriyā—on the right side. Salutation to Śānti—on the left foot. Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to Dānti—on the right foot.

Salutation to Dayā—on the right hand. Salutation to Śraddhā—on the left hand. (l. 5) Salutation to Dvitīyā—on the right breast. Salutation to Bandhā—on the left breast. Having worshipped with "Salutation to Rātrī," one should place [these] in the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*).

To Īśāna, who is crystal-colored, whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, who is in a dancing form, and whose quality is tranquility: *oṃ hrīṃ umāyai namaḥ*. To Tatpuruṣa, who is yellow-colored, whose hand holds a serpent, who possesses supreme beauty, and whose quality is *rudra*: *hrīṃ gaurīyai namaḥ* || 2 ||
Oṃ, homage to Aghora, who has the color of collyrium, who wields a bow, who is most terrifying, and who holds a sword and a shield in his hands; hrīṃ, homage to Gaṅgā. 3.
Oṃ, homage to Vāmadeva, who is red in color, seated in a blissful posture, holding a noose and a goad in his hands, and possessing a fierce form; and to Ambikā, hrīṃ! 4.
Oṃ, salutation to Sadyojāta, who is white in color, who holds a trident, a noose, and a goad in his hands, who possesses a fierce form; hrīṃ, salutation to Gaṇāmbikā. 5.
Oṃ, to the heart, to the fire-splendor, to the one whose nature is knowledge, to the one with hands granting fearlessness and boons, to Hrīṃ Vāminī, obeisance! 6.

Oṃ, to the head, to the splendor of Īśāna, to the one of yellow complexion, to the three-eyed one, to the one with the trident and skull, to the one with hands in the boon-granting gesture: Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Kriyā. 7.

Oṃ, homage to the one who is the armor, red in color, whose deity is Vāyu, who has three eyes, and who holds a trident, a skull-bowl, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness; to the wielder of the *khaṭvāṅga*, Hrīṃ, homage! 8.

To the one who possesses weapons, whose limbs are black, who has three eyes, who holds a trident and a skull-bowl, and who bestows boons and fearlessness: *hrīṃ*, obeisance to Gaṅgā. The second enclosure (*dvitīyāvaraṇa*): obeisance to Vāmā; obeisance to Jyeṣṭhā; obeisance to Raudrī; obeisance to Kālī; obeisance to Kalavikaraṇī; obeisance to Balavikaraṇī; obeisance to Balapramathanī; obeisance to Sarvabhūtadamanī; obeisance to Manonmanī.
The third enclosure: Salutation to Ambikā; salutation to Gaṇāmbikā; salutation to Gaṅgā; salutation to Gaurī; salutation to Umā; salutation to Devī; salutation to Īśvarī; salutation to Manonmanī.

The fourth enclosure: Salutation to Brāhmī; salutation to Māheśvarī; salutation to Kāmārī; salutation to Vaiṣṇavī; salutation to Vārāhī; salutation to Māhendrī; salutation to Cāmuṇḍī; salutation to Durgā; salutation to Mahālakṣmī; salutation to Sarasvatī.

The five obstructions (*pañcāvaraṇa*): homage to the sword; homage to the noose; homage to the goad; homage to the hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*); homage to the skull-bowl; homage to the banner-cloth; homage to the *vetāla*; homage to the razor-knife; homage to the trident; homage to the staff (*gada*); homage to the mirror; homage to the full vase; homage to the lion; homage to the pair of syllables; homage to the *śrīvatsa*; homage to the *svastika*.

Having worshipped with "Oṃ Śaṅkha... namaḥ," [one worships] with: "Oṃ Rambhāyai namaḥ," "Oṃ Tilottamāyai namaḥ," "Oṃ Sumukhi(khī) namaḥ," "Oṃ Sundarī namaḥ," "Oṃ Durmukhi(khī) namaḥ," "Oṃ Kāmavardhanī namaḥ," "Oṃ Pūjanī namaḥ," and "Oṃ Śobhāyai namaḥ. Having thus worshipped, one should perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) in the lotus-pit (*padmakuṇḍa*) in the four directions starting from the east, and in the womb-pit (*yonikuṇḍa*) between the northeast and the wheel. [One recites]: "Oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ hūṃ bhāṃ bhīṃ indrāyai namaḥ."

Kālī, salutations again and again! Oṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ hoṃ, salutations to Bhadrā; Kālī, salutations again and again! Having drawn forth the vital breath from the eyes, ears, tongue, nose, speech, feet, hands, anus, thighs, and private parts, [salutations] to Bhadranālī.
(The installation of the left-hand form—meditation: Dhyāna: (p. 74b, f. 90a, l. 1)
Now I shall describe specifically the installation of the right-facing form,
which bestows enjoyment at all times, grants all boons, and yields the fruit of all sacrifices.
Sacrifice bestows knowledge, wealth, and the destruction of enemies;
[it should be performed] for the gods during the daytime on an auspicious day in the bright fortnight.
One should commence the installation when joined with an auspicious weekday and so forth;
one should perform the offering of the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) on the day prior to the day of the consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
O Vedayā, prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with rice grains in the beautiful pavilion;
upon that, place the pinnacle (*kūṭa*), provided it is joined with the door-posts.
The wise one should perform the deposition of jewels according to the previously stated rule.
O Prajāpati, when the installation of the jewels has failed,
one should perform the opening of the eyes under the constellation *Pakṣinetra*.
Having prepared the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) as before, one should place the image (*bera*) upon it.
Having placed the sages, Kauśika and the others, in order on the right side,
the preceptor [should perform] the rite of speech with fine [threads], by means of striking with a golden needle.
Then one should perform the opening of the eyes, joined with the Netra-mantra;
one should perform each respective act while recollecting the specific eye of each of the Ṛṣis.
Thereafter, one should worship Takṣaka with garments, gold, and rings;
having driven away Takṣaka, prepare the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to his east.
Having placed the deity upon it, [and] the ṛṣis to the right,
one should sprinkle them with pure water while reciting the respective mantra for each person.
One should satisfy them in sequence with honey as well, even with those [offerings] that have protruding nails;
taking each of the previously mentioned vessels filled with a *prastha* [of liquid].
The wise one should fill it with ghee and honey as before;
then, reciting the respective mantra, the supreme instructor should display it.
...and the limbs, O Brahmins, according to the sequence of the heap of grain.

One should then show [the image] to the Lord of Gods (*deveśa*) with water mixed with the eight kinds of clay. Afterward, one should show it to the sages (*ṛṣi*) with water mixed with the eight kinds of clay.
One should likewise bathe [the image] with the fifth [substance] for the sages (*ṛṣis*).
One should wrap the image—which is provided with a long beard—in a cloth;
adorned with all ornaments, one should circumambulate it from left to right through the village of the animals (*tiryaggrāma*).
Having entered the water’s edge, one should establish [the deity] upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
Having formed a lotus in the midst of the water, one should place Śiva in its center.
To the north of him, one should lay the Ṛṣis, and to the south, one should lay them with their respective mantras.
One should construct a pavilion on the top of the palace according to the previously mentioned procedure.
In the middle of that, one should construct an auspicious paved floor (*kuṭṭima*) equal in size to the area for eating;
and having made great sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*) in the hearts [of the deities] in due order.
One should likewise fashion a square, a quadrangular, a hollow-cornered, and a circular [mandala] according to the great scriptures; thus, a lotus is to be arranged in the corners.
Between Indra and Īśāna, one should construct a well-rounded primary pedestal (*pradhānaka*) as a bathing altar (*snānavedikā*) according to the path prescribed for the installation of the *liṅga*;
having removed the carpenter, one should smear it with cow dung and other materials.
One should have the mantra and the *puṇyāha* recited and feed the Brahmins there.
Then, having removed the remnants of the meal, one should sprinkle the pavilion with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Afterward, one should worship the pavilion according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Then one should perform the *vāstuhoma* and carry out the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*).
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the center of the altar (*vedikā*), one should draw a lotus.
One should arrange a bed there and worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having emerged from the water, one should place the images (beras) in due order in the area designated for bathing.
Then, having removed the pits and other such things, one should perform purification as before.
One should cause the water for the feet, the water for sipping, and the respectful offering to be given with the Sadyojāta mantra respectively.
Having worshipped with incense, flowers, and so forth, using the respective Īśāna-mantras,
one should then display the lotus-mudrā and subsequently display that which is called Maheśa. [One should] display the Surabhī-mudrā for the sages beginning with Kaśyapa.
One should sever [the hair] together with the long beard, cutting it separately for each face.
Then, having bound the protective amulet (*kautuka*) with the respective heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*),
one should lay the deity upon the bed, facing either east, west, or upward.
One should cause the deity and the Ṛṣi to lie down on the right and left respectively;
each should be wrapped individually in a red cloth while reciting the Heart-mantra.
One should place the Śiva-pitcher on the right side of the head;
then, on his left hand...
...but one should place those respective [substances] on the head-part of the pitcher.
One should then install the pitchers of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) around it in due order,
equipped with grass-brooms (*kūrca*), provided with lids, and filled with water containing *gaṇa*-herbs.
One should wrap each [vessel] individually with cloth, together with the sūtras and sprouts.
... One should place five jewels and a golden lotus in the *vardhanī*, and a piece of gold for the ṛṣis, depositing them with their respective mantras.
One should meditate upon the form of Maheśa and place his respective mantra in the pitcher;
then, assuming the form of Gaurī, one should place her mantra in the water-pot.
One should display the *mukula* and the *padma-mudrā* with both hands;
then, having worshipped with incense, flowers, and so forth, one should cause the food offering (*naivedya*) to be presented.

Regarding the cause:

It is prescribed for the month of Vaiśākha, Śrāvaṇa, or alternatively Phālguna; on an auspicious weekday, under a favorable lunar mansion, at a good moment, and in a favorable ascendant.
In the *Svāyambhuva*:
"When the sun faces north and so forth, it is called the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*);
likewise, when the sun faces south, it is the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*)."
The period up to the movement of the sun [to the next sign] is proclaimed as an *ayana*;
that which begins with the month of Puṣya and extends to the end of Caitra is called the *pūrvāhṇa*.
That which begins with Caitra and ends with Taurus (*vṛṣa*) is proclaimed as the *aparāhṇa*.
The period beginning from the month of Puṣya up to the month of Caitra is traditionally known as the "early night" (pūrvarātra).
The period from the month of Āśvina to Puṣya is known as Apararātra.
